newsitem.title: EGYPT: Arabs say peace lost, Israeli intransigence won.
newsitem.headline: Arabs say peace lost, Israeli intransigence won.

text.p: Arabs dismissed on Thursday the Middle East summit in Washington as a failure for peace and a victory for Israeli intransigence.
Some predicted it could lead only to further violence in the Palestinian territories, where 73 people have died since clashes between Palestinians and Israeli troops erupted last week.
"The summit has failed because of Israeli intransigence," said Hasan Asfour, a PLO negotiator.
Mustafa Natsheh, the Palestinian mayor of Hebron, where 400 Jewish settlers live among 100,000 Palestinians, said the peace process was on the verge of collapse.
"Unless international and Arab public opinion and Israeli peace groups move, the area will not witness any calm and the cycle of violence will return anew," he said.

The Washington summit, attended by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and King Hussein of Jordan, ended on Wednesday without agreement on any of the substantial points the Arabs wanted settled.
Israel and the Palestinians agreed only to end violence and keep talking about matters the Palestinians thought they agreed with the Israelis a year ago.

"It is clear that the Israelis did not come to Washington to make progress... The proposals submitted by the Israeli delegation constitute a total retreat from the framework of peace," said Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa.
"The whole exercise ended in more promises, more pledges. But promises and pledges by Netanyahu are not enough, what we need is deeds," added a senior Egyptian official.
"If there are no moves, it will be a catastrophe... Throwing stones (by the Palestinians) will look mild in comparison to what might happen," he added.
"(The summit) will leave Palestinians with one option, to return to the fight," said the Saudi newspaper al-Madina.
Another Gulf newspaper, al-Khaleej in the United Arab Emirates, echoed the theme that three months after he took office, Netanyahu had shown he was not to be trusted.
"The Palestinians received a bunch of promises...that will soon be broken, one promise after the other, on the tables of negotiation with Netanyahu, the biggest liar," it said.
Syria, one of the most vociferous Arab critics of Netanyahu's concept of peace, said the summit showed the time had come for Arabs to carry out threats to end normalisation.
"The Washington summit has totally failed to find any solution for the disputes between the Palestinians and the Israelis," said the official Syrian newspaper al-Baath.
"Arabs should not waste time waiting for any gesture from Netanyahu's government... They should sever ties with Israel and freeze the multilateral talks," it added.

"Netanyahu wanted the Washington summit to adopt his style of negotiations based on nothing for Arabs. He wanted the Washington summit to reward the aggressor for killing his victim and endorsing his occupation of Arab lands," it said.

Only in Egypt and Jordan, the Arab states which have signed peace treaties with the Jewish states, was there any sympathy for U.S. President Bill Clinton, the summit host, or willingness to see anything positive in the meeting.
"He did his maximum... He took a risk and we appreciate that," said the senior Egyptian official.
In Jordan headlines on most state-controlled newspapers, using red ink letters, blamed Netanyahu for the failure.
Government officials said the outcome was below expectations but at least managed to put talks back on track.
"Certainly the summit was below expectations but at least it averted a disaster for the time being and left an opening for Palestinians and Israelis to continue talks," said one.

"In an election year for Clinton, who has to rely on Jewish votes, no sane person should have expected much to come out of the summit anyway," said Samir Mohammad, 31, an office assistant resident in Amman but originally from Jerusalem.
"My only hope now is for Jordan and Egypt to stand together and take some steps, even if they are only symbolic ones, to further isolate Netanyahu," he added.
At Mar Elias refugee camp in Beirut, Palestinians had few kind words for Arafat, widely seen elsewhere as the victim.

"We warned Arafat not to go to Washington as long as Israel does not commit itself to closing the tunnel (in Jerusalem) and stopping settlements. We condemn Arafat's policies," said Fathi Kulaib, press officer for the radical Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine.

"Arafat sold us all. He does not represent us any more and we do not care about his negotiations with the Israelis. We have finally realised that we sacrificed our children for nothing," said Um Wissam, a 47-year-old housewife.
